title: Living for someone else
hook: Seneca cares for his health for his wife Paulina's sake (Letters 104)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was consolatio, and a stern letter to a grieving father. Your line was gentler than seneca.

Here's a small scene from a marriage. One of you is getting sick, and wants to push through. The other says: please, just go and rest. And you go, not because you're convinced, but because you can see the worry on their face. In the hundred-and-fourth letter, Seneca feels a fever coming on in Rome, and leaves for his farm at Nomentum, outside the city. His wife Paulina, he says, keeps urging him to look after his health. On the way, he thinks about what we owe our own bodies when someone else depends on us.
screen: `PLEASE, JUST GO AND REST.` → `A FEVER IN ROME.` → `PAULINA'S WORRY.`

segments.voice: First, Paulina. Seneca says she kept urging him to look after his health. And because he knows, he writes, that her life is bound up with his, he has begun to take care of himself in order to take care of her. Old age had made him bolder about many things, he admits, and careless about his body. For her sake, he lets that go. Second, the indulgence. He calls this an honest indulgence, a soft spot he isn't ashamed of. Some people think the wise should be indifferent to their own health. Seneca says no: a good person will sometimes hold on to life, and look after it, for the sake of those they love, even when they'd personally shrug. Third, the larger point. Caring for yourself isn't always selfish. Sometimes it's a gift. A parent who sees a doctor, a friend who finally sleeps, a partner who takes the medicine: they're doing it for someone. Fourth, the history. Tacitus, the Roman historian, tells us Paulina outlived Seneca by a few years, and kept an honored memory of her husband. Her name is still attached to this kindness in a letter. Tomorrow, the same letter turns to Socrates.
screen: `PAULINA URGES HIM TO REST.` · `AN HONEST INDULGENCE.` · `SELF-CARE CAN BE GENEROUS.` · `PAULINA'S NAME, STILL IN THE LETTER.` · then, large: `FOR PAULINA.`

segments.voice: Think of one person who'd be affected if you didn't look after yourself, a partner, a child, a friend, even a pet who waits by the door, and picture their face. Then think of one small care you've let slide, sleep, a checkup, a walk, and imagine doing it for their sake, as a gift rather than a chore.
Honesta indulgentia. Seneca's phrase for caring for his own health, for his wife Paulina's sake, and calling it an honest indulgence he isn't ashamed of. Today's word.
Your line: for paulina. Looking after yourself can be a kindness to someone else. That's day four hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Readers of this letter often think of looking after their own health as something they do for the people who depend on them, not only for themselves.

chat.says: Isn't taking care of your own health kind of selfish?
options: Not always; Seneca looked after himself for Paulina's sake, so care can be a gift.
Yes; Seneca said the wise should ignore their health and push through anything.

chat.meaning: Seneca says he began caring for himself to care for Paulina, whose life was bound up with his. He called it an honest indulgence.

Paulina.meaning: Seneca's wife, who urged him to look after his health

Nomentum.meaning: a town outside Rome where Seneca had a farm

Tacitus.meaning: a Roman historian who wrote about Seneca and Nero

honesta indulgentia.meaning: Latin: an honest indulgence, a soft spot without shame

notes: Letters 104.1: fever, leaving for Nomentum, Paulina's attempt to keep him. 104.2: 'cum sciam spiritum illius in meo verti, incipio, ut illi consulam, mihi consulere'; old age had made him braver about many things. 104.3–4: one must sometimes hold on to life for loved ones; 'honesta indulgentia'. Confirm wording; the script says only that Paulina urged him to look after his health.

104.3 also says the good man should live not as long as he pleases but as long as he ought, in a context touching on suicide; the script phrases this gently and does not mention ending life. Sensitivity check welcome.
Tacitus, Annals 15.63–64: Paulina's attempt to die with Seneca is omitted; the script mentions only that she outlived him by a few years ('paucos annos... laudabili in maritum memoria'). Confirm.
